verses.zh: 回答柔和，使怒消退；言语暴戾，触动怒气。
verses.en: A gentle response[NOTE:1] turns away anger,but a harsh word[NOTE:2] stirs up wrath.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “soft answer.” The adjective רַךְ (rakh, “soft; tender; gentle”; BDB 940 s.v.) is more than a mild response; it is conciliatory, an answer that restores good temper and reasonableness (W. McKane, Proverbs [OTL], 477). Gideon illustrates this kind of answer (Judg 8:1-3) that brings peace.

Heb “word of harshness”; KJV “grievous words.” The noun עֶצֶב (ʿetsev, “pain, hurt”) functions as an attributive genitive. The term עֶצֶב refers to something that causes pain (BDB 780 s.v. I עֶצֶב). For example, Jephthah’s harsh answer led to war (Judg 12:1-6).
Heb “raises anger.” A common response to painful words is to let one’s temper flare up.

verses.zh: 智慧人的舌善发知识；愚昧人的口吐出愚昧。
verses.en: The tongue of the wise[NOTE:1] treats knowledge correctly,[NOTE:2] but the mouth of the fool spouts out[NOTE:3] folly.
notes: The contrast is between the “tongue of the wise” and the “mouth of the fool.” Both expressions are metonymies of cause; the subject matter is what they say. How wise people are can be determined from what they say.

Or “makes knowledge acceptable” (so NASB). The verb תֵּיטִיב (tetiv, Hiphil imperfect of יָטַב [yatav, “to be good”]) can be translated “to make good” or “to treat in a good [or, excellent] way” (C. H. Toy, Proverbs [ICC], 303). M. Dahood, however, suggests emending the text to תֵּיטִיף (tetif) which is a cognate of נָטַף (nataf, “drip”), and translates “tongues of the sages drip with knowledge” (Proverbs and Northwest Semitic Philology, 32-33). But this change is gratuitous and unnecessary.
The Hiphil verb יַבִּיעַ (yabbiaʿ) means “to pour out; to emit; to cause to bubble; to belch forth.” The fool bursts out with reckless utterances (cf. TEV “spout nonsense”).

verses.zh: 耶和华的眼目无处不在；恶人善人，他都鉴察。
verses.en: The eyes of the Lord[NOTE:1] are in every place,keeping watch on[NOTE:2] those who are evil and those who are good.
notes: The proverb uses anthropomorphic language to describe God’s exacting and evaluating knowledge of all people.
The form צֹפוֹת (tsofot, “watching”) is a feminine plural participle agreeing with “eyes.” God’s watching eyes comfort good people but convict evil.

verses.zh: 温良的舌是生命树；乖谬的嘴使人心碎。
verses.en: Speech[NOTE:1] that heals[NOTE:2] is like[NOTE:3] a life-giving tree,[NOTE:4] but a perverse speech[NOTE:5] breaks the spirit.[NOTE:6]
notes: Heb “a tongue.” The term “tongue” is a metonymy of cause for what is produced: speech.
Heb “a tongue of healing.” A healing tongue refers to speech that is therapeutic or soothing. It is a source of vitality.
The comparative “like” does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is implied by the metaphor; it is supplied for the sake of clarity.
Heb “tree of life.”

Heb “perversion in it.” The referent must be the tongue, representing speech, from the first line; so this has been supplied in the translation for clarity. A tongue that is twisted, perverse, or deceitful is a way of describing deceitful speech. Such words will crush the spirit.
Heb “is a fracture in the spirit.”

verses.zh: 愚妄人藐视父亲的管教；领受责备的，得着见识。
verses.en: A fool rejects his father’s discipline,but whoever heeds reproof shows good sense.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “is prudent” (so KJV, NASB, NRSV); NCV, NLT “is wise.” Anyone who accepts correction or rebuke will become prudent in life.

verses.zh: 义人家中多有财宝；恶人得利反受扰害。
verses.en: In the house of the righteous is abundant wealth,[NOTE:1] but the income of the wicked will be ruined.[NOTE:2]
notes: The Hebrew noun חֹסֶן (khosen) means “wealth; treasure.” Prosperity is the reward for righteousness. This is true only in so far as a proverb can be carried in its application, allowing for exceptions. The Greek text for this verse has no reference for wealth, but talks about amassing righteousness.

Heb “being ruined.” The Niphal participle of עָכַר (ʿakhar; “to disturb, trouble, ruin”) may be understood substantivally, meaning “disturbance, calamity” (BDB 747 s.v. עָכַר) or a “thing troubled,” thus perhaps “[it] is ruined/ruinous.” Or it may be viewed verbally, “will be ruined” (HALOT 824 s.v. עכר nif). The LXX translates “will be ruined.”

verses.zh: 智慧人的嘴播扬知识；愚昧人的心并不如此。
verses.en: The lips of the wise spread[NOTE:1] knowledge,but not so the heart of fools.[NOTE:2]
notes: The verb of the first colon, יְזָרוּ (yezaru, “they scatter”) is difficult because it does not fit the second very well—a heart does not “scatter” or “spread” knowledge. Symmachus’ Greek translation uses φυλάσσω (phulassō, “to guard, keep”) suggesting his text read יִצְּרוּ (yitseru) from נָצַר (natsar, “to guard, keep watch, comply with”). The LXX uses a form of δέω (deō, “to bind”). Although binding (often being bound as a prisoner) might be related to guarding, δέω does not otherwise represent נָצַר in the LXX. Still the editors of BHS and C. H. Toy (Proverbs [ICC], 305) suggest reading יִצְּרוּ (yitseru, “they guard”).

The Hebrew לֹא־כֵן (loʾ khen) could be “not so” (HALOT 482 s.v. II כֵּן) or “not right, incorrect, wrong” (HALOT 482 s.v. I כֵּן), which is supported by the LXX: “hearts of fools are unstable.” If לֵב (lev, “heart, mind”) is understood to represent thinking, then, accepting the emendation in the first line, the proverb may say, “The lips of the wise preserve knowledge, but the thoughts of fools are incorrect.”sn The phrase “the heart of fools” emphasizes that fools do not comprehend knowledge. Cf. NCV “there is no knowledge in the thoughts of fools.”

verses.zh: 恶人献祭，为耶和华所憎恶；正直人祈祷，为他所喜悦。
verses.en: The Lord abhors[NOTE:1] the sacrifice of the wicked,[NOTE:2] but the prayer[NOTE:3] of the upright pleases him.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “an abomination of the Lord.” The term יְהוָה (yehvah, “the Lord”) functions as a subjective genitive: “the Lord abhors.” Cf. NIV “the Lord detests”; NCV, NLT “the Lord hates”; CEV “the Lord is disgusted.”

The sacrifices of the wicked are hated by the Lord because the worshipers are insincere and blasphemous (e.g., Prov 15:29; 21:3; 28:9; Ps 40:6-8; Isa 1:10-17). In other words, the spiritual condition of the worshiper determines whether or not the worship is acceptable to God.

J. H. Greenstone notes that if God will accept the prayers of the upright, he will accept their sacrifices; for sacrifice is an outer ritual and easily performed even by the wicked, but prayer is a private and inward act and not usually fabricated by unbelievers (Proverbs, 162).
Heb “[is] his pleasure.” The third person masculine singular suffix functions as a subjective genitive: “he is pleased.” God is pleased with the prayers of the upright.

verses.zh: 恶人的道路，为耶和华所憎恶；追求公义的，为他所喜爱。
verses.en: The Lord abhors[NOTE:1] the way of the wicked,but he will love[NOTE:2] those[NOTE:3] who pursue[NOTE:4] righteousness.
notes: Heb “an abomination of the Lord.” The term יְהוָה (yehvah, “the Lord”) functions as a subjective genitive: “the Lord abhors.”
The verb אָהֵב (ʾahev, “to love”) is stative, so its imperfect form should be future; it still speaks of a general truth.
Heb “the one who” (so NRSV).

God hates the way of the wicked, that is, their lifestyle and things they do. God loves those who pursue righteousness, the Piel verb signifying a persistent pursuit. W. G. Plaut says, “He who loves God will be moved to an active, persistent, and even dangerous search for justice” (Proverbs, 170).

verses.zh: 舍弃正路的，必受严刑；恨恶责备的，必致死亡。
verses.en: Severe discipline[NOTE:1] is for the one who abandons the way;the one who hates reproof[NOTE:2] will die.
notes: The two lines are parallel synonymously, so the “severe discipline” of the first colon is parallel to “will die” of the second. The expression מוּסָר רָע (musar raʿ, “severe discipline”) indicates a discipline that is catastrophic or harmful to life.

If this line and the previous line are synonymous, then the one who abandons the way also refuses any correction, and so there is severe punishment. To abandon the way means to leave the life of righteousness which is the repeated subject of the book of Proverbs.

verses.zh: 阴间和灭亡尚在耶和华眼前，何况世人的心呢？
verses.en: Death and Destruction[NOTE:1] are before the Lord—how much more[NOTE:2] the hearts of humans![NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “Sheol and Abaddon” (שְׁאוֹל וַאֲבַדּוֹן (sheʾol vaʾavaddon); so ASV, NASB, NRSV; cf. KJV “Hell and destruction”; NAB “the nether world and the abyss.” These terms represent the remote underworld and all the mighty powers that reside there (e.g., Prov 27:20; Job 26:6; Ps 139:8; Amos 9:2; Rev 9:11). The Lord knows everything about this remote region.

The construction אַף כִּי (ʾaf ki, “how much more!”) introduces an argument from the lesser to the greater: If all this is open before the Lord, how much more so human hearts. “Hearts” here is a metonymy of subject, meaning the motives and thoughts (cf. NCV “the thoughts of the living”).
Heb “the hearts of the sons of man,” although here “sons of man” simply means “men” or “human beings.”

verses.zh: 亵慢人不爱受责备；他也不就近智慧人。
verses.en: The scorner will not love[NOTE:1] one who corrects him;[NOTE:2] he will not go to[NOTE:3] the wise.
notes: The verb אָהֵב (ʾahev, “to love”) is stative, so its imperfect form should be future tense.sn This is an understatement, the opposite being intended (a figure called tapeinosis). A scorner rejects any efforts to reform him.

The form הוֹכֵחַ (hokheakh) is a Hiphil infinitive absolute. It could function as the object of the verb (cf. NIV, NRSV) or as a finite verb (cf. KJV, NASB, NLT). The latter has been chosen here because of the prepositional phrase following it, although that is not a conclusive argument.
The MT has אֶל (ʾel, “to [the wise]”), suggesting seeking the advice of the wise. The LXX, however, has “with the wise,” suggesting אֶת (ʾet).

verses.zh: 心中喜乐，面带笑容；心里忧愁，灵被损伤。
verses.en: A joyful heart[NOTE:1] makes the face cheerful,[NOTE:2] but by a painful heart the spirit is broken.
notes: The contrast in this proverb is between the “joyful heart” (Heb “a heart of joy,” using an attributive genitive) and the “painful heart” (Heb “pain of the heart,” using a genitive of specification).

The verb יֵיטִב (yetiv) normally means “to make good,” but here “to make the face good,” that is, there is a healthy, favorable, uplifted expression. The antithesis is the pained heart that crushes the spirit. C. H. Toy observes that a broken spirit is expressed by a sad face, while a cheerful face shows a courageous spirit (Proverbs [ICC], 308).

verses.zh: 聪明人心求知识；愚昧人口吃愚昧。
verses.en: The discerning mind[NOTE:1] seeks knowledge,but the mouth of fools feeds on folly.[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “heart.” The Hebrew term is לֵב (lev, “mind, heart”).

The idea expressed in the second colon does not make a strong parallelism with the first with its emphasis on seeking knowledge. Its poetic image of feeding (a hypocatastasis) would signify the acquisition of folly—the fool has an appetite for it. D. W. Thomas suggests the change of one letter, ר (resh) to ד (dalet), to obtain a reading יִדְעֶה (yidʿeh); this he then connects to an Arabic root daʿa with the meaning “sought, demanded” to form what he thinks is a better parallel (“Textual and Philological Notes on Some Passages in the Book of Proverbs,” VTSup 3 [1955]: 285). But even though the parallelism is not as precise as some would prefer, there is insufficient warrant for such a change.

verses.zh: 困苦人的日子都是愁苦；心中欢畅的，常享丰筵。
verses.en: All the days[NOTE:1] of the afflicted[NOTE:2] are bad,[NOTE:3] but one with[NOTE:4] a cheerful heart has a continual feast.[NOTE:5]
notes: The “days” represent what happens on those days (metonymy of subject).

The contrast is between the “afflicted” and the “good of heart” (a genitive of specification, “cheerful/healthy heart/spirit/attitude”). sn The parallelism suggests that the afflicted is one afflicted within his spirit, for the proverb is promoting a healthy frame of mind.
Or “evil”; or “catastrophic.”
“one with” is supplied.

The image of a continual feast signifies the enjoyment of what life offers (cf. TEV “happy people…enjoy life”). The figure is a hypocatastasis; among its several implications are joy, fulfillment, abundance, pleasure.

verses.zh: 少有财宝，敬畏耶和华，强如多有财宝，烦乱不安。
verses.en: Better[NOTE:1] is little with the fear of the Lordthan great wealth and turmoil[NOTE:2] with it.[NOTE:3]
notes: One of the frequent characteristics of wisdom literature is the “better” saying; it is a comparison of different but similar things to determine which is to be preferred. These two verses focus on spiritual things being better than troubled material things.
Turmoil refers to anxiety; the fear of the Lord alleviates anxiety, for it brings with it contentment and confidence.

Not all wealth has turmoil with it. But the proverb is focusing on the comparison of two things—fear of the Lord with little and wealth with turmoil. Between these two, the former is definitely better.

verses.zh: 吃素菜，彼此相爱，强如吃肥牛，彼此相恨。
verses.en: Better a meal of vegetables where there is love[NOTE:1] than a fattened ox where there is hatred.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and love there.” This clause is a circumstantial clause introduced with vav, that becomes “where there is love.” The same construction is used in the second colon.

Again the saying concerns troublesome wealth: Loving relationships with simple food are better than a feast where there is hatred. The ideal, of course, would be loving family and friends with a great meal in addition, but this proverb is only comparing two things.

verses.zh: 暴怒的人挑启争端；忍怒的人止息纷争。
verses.en: A quick-tempered person[NOTE:1] stirs up dissension,but one who is slow to anger[NOTE:2] calms[NOTE:3] a quarrel.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “a man of wrath”; KJV, ASV “a wrathful man.” The term “wrath” functions as an attributive genitive: “an angry person.” He is contrasted with the “slow of anger,” so he is a “quick-tempered person” (cf. NLT “a hothead”).
Heb “slow of anger.” The noun “anger” functions as a genitive of specification: slow in reference to anger, that is, slow to get angry, patient.

The Hiphil verb יַשְׁקִיט (yashqit) means “to cause quietness; to pacify; to allay” the strife or quarrel (cf. NAB “allays discord”). This type of person goes out of his way to keep things calm and minimize contention; his opposite thrives on disagreement and dispute.

The fact that רִיב (riv) is used for “quarrel; strife” strongly implies that the setting is the courtroom or other legal setting (the gates of the city). The hot-headed person is eager to turn every disagreement into a legal case.

verses.zh: 懒惰人的道像荆棘的篱笆；正直人的路是平坦的大道。
verses.en: The way of the sluggard is like a hedge of thorns,[NOTE:1] but the path of the upright is like[NOTE:2] a highway.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “like an overgrowth”; NRSV “overgrown with thorns”; cf. CEV “like walking in a thorn patch.” The point of the simile is that the path of life taken by the lazy person has many obstacles that are painful—it is like trying to break through a hedge of thorns. The LXX has “strewn with thorns.”
The comparative “like” does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is implied by the metaphor; it is supplied for the sake of clarity.

The contrast to the “thorny way” is the highway, the Hebrew word signifying a well built-up road (סָלַל, salal, “to heap up”). The upright have no reason to swerve, duck, or detour, but may expect “clear sailing.” Prov 28:19 pairs similar concepts while Prov 6:10 and 10:26 speak of the hardships associated with laziness.

verses.zh: 智慧子使父亲喜乐；愚昧人藐视母亲。
verses.en: A wise child[NOTE:1] brings joy to his father,but a foolish person[NOTE:2] despises[NOTE:3] his mother.
notes: Heb “son.”
Heb “a fool of a man,” a genitive of specification.
The proverb is almost the same as 10:1, except that “despises” replaces “grief.” This adds the idea of the callousness of the one who inflicts grief on his mother (D. Kidner, Proverbs [TOTC], 116).

verses.zh: 无知的人以愚妄为乐；聪明的人按正直而行。
verses.en: Folly is a joy to one who lacks sense,[NOTE:1] but one who has understanding[NOTE:2] follows an upright course.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “lacking of mind.” The term לֵב (lev, “mind, heart”) refers by metonymy to thinking, and by extension to discernment, wisdom, good sense (cf. NIV84 “judgment”; NIV11 “sense”). The one who has not developed this ability to make proper choices finds great delight in folly.
Heb “a man of understanding” (so KJV, NIV84); NIV11 “whoever has understanding”; NLT “a sensible person.”

The Hebrew construction is יְיַשֶּׁר־לָכֶת (yeyasher lakhet, “makes straight [to] go”). This is a verbal hendiadys, in which the first verb, the Piel imperfect, becomes adverbial, and the second form, the infinitive construct of הָלַךְ, halakh, becomes the main verb: “goes straight ahead” (cf. NRSV).

verses.zh: 不先商议，所谋无效；谋士众多，所谋乃成。
verses.en: Plans fail[NOTE:1] when there is no counsel,but with abundant advisers they are established.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “go wrong” (so NRSV, NLT). The verb is the Hiphil infinitive absolute from פָּרַר, parar, which means “to break; to frustrate; to go wrong” (HALOT 975 s.v. I פרר 2). The plans are made ineffectual or are frustrated when there is insufficient counsel.
The proverb says essentially the same thing as 11:14, but differently.

verses.zh: 口善应对，自觉喜乐；话合其时，何等美好。
verses.en: A person has joy[NOTE:1] in giving an appropriate answer,[NOTE:2] and a word at the right time[NOTE:3]—how good it is!
notes: Heb “joy to the man” or “the man has joy.”

Heb “in the answer of his mouth” (so ASV); NASB “in an apt answer.” The term “mouth” is a metonymy of cause for what he says. But because the parallelism is loosely synonymous, the answer given here must be equal to the good word spoken in season. So it is an answer that is proper or fitting.
Heb “in its season.” To say the right thing at the right time is useful; to say the right thing at the wrong time is counterproductive.

verses.zh: 智慧人从生命的道上升，使他远离在下的阴间。
verses.en: The path of life is upward[NOTE:1] for the wise person,[NOTE:2] to[NOTE:3] keep him from going downward to Sheol.[NOTE:4]
notes: There is disagreement over the meaning of the term translated “upward.” The verse is usually taken to mean that “upward” is a reference to physical life and well-being (cf. NCV), and “going down to Sheol” is a reference to physical death, that is, the grave, because the concept of immortality is said not to appear in the book of Proverbs. The proverb then would mean that the wise live long and healthy lives. But W. McKane argues (correctly) that “upwards” in contrast to Sheol, does not fit the ways of describing the worldly pattern of conduct and that it is only intelligible if taken as a reference to immortality (Proverbs [OTL], 480). The translations “upwards” and “downwards” are not found in the LXX. This has led some commentators to speculate that these terms were not found in the original, but were added later, after the idea of immortality became prominent. However, this is mere speculation.
Heb “to the wise [man],” because the form is masculine.
The term לְמַעַן (lemaʿan, “in order to”) introduces a purpose clause; the path leads upward in order to turn the wise away from Sheol.
Heb “to turn from Sheol downward”; cf. NAB “the nether world below.”

verses.zh: 耶和华必拆毁骄傲人的家，却要立定寡妇的地界。
verses.en: The Lord tears down the house of the proud,[NOTE:1] but he maintains the boundaries of the widow.[NOTE:2]
notes: The “proud” have to be understood here in contrast to the widow, and their “house” has to be interpreted in contrast to the widow’s territory. The implication may be that the “proud” make their gain from the needy, and so God will set the balance right.

The Lord administers justice in his time. The Lord champions the widow, the orphan, the poor, and the needy. These people were often the prey of the proud, who would take and devour their houses and lands (e.g., 1 Kgs 21; Prov 16:19; Isa 5:8-10).

verses.zh: 恶谋为耶和华所憎恶；良言乃为纯净。
verses.en: The Lord abhors[NOTE:1] the plans[NOTE:2] of the wicked,[NOTE:3] but pleasant words[NOTE:4] are pure.[NOTE:5]
notes: Heb “an abomination of the Lord.” The term יְהוָה (yehvah, “the Lord”) functions as a subjective genitive: “the Lord abhors.”

The noun מַחְשְׁבוֹת (makhshevot) means “thoughts” (so KJV, NIV, NLT), from the verb חָשַׁב (khashav, “to think; to reckon; to devise”). So these are intentions, what is being planned (cf. NAB “schemes”).
The word רַע (raʿ, “evil, wicked”) is a genitive of source or subjective genitive, meaning the plans that the wicked devise—“wicked plans.”

The contrast is between the “thoughts” and the “words.” The thoughts that are designed to hurt people the Lord hates; words that are pleasant (נֹעַם, noʿam), however, are pure (to him). What is pleasant is delightful, lovely, enjoyable.

The MT simply has “but pleasant words are pure” (Heb “but pure [plural] are the words of pleasantness”). Some English versions add “to him” or “in his sight” to make the connection to the first part (cf. NAB, NIV). The LXX has: “the sayings of the pure are held in honor.” The Vulgate has: “pure speech will be confirmed by him as very beautiful.” The NIV84 has paraphrased here: “but those of the pure are pleasing to him”; NIV11 reads: “but gracious words are pure in his sight.”

verses.zh: 贪恋财利的，扰害己家；恨恶贿赂的，必得存活。
verses.en: The one who is greedy for gain[NOTE:1] troubles[NOTE:2] his household,[NOTE:3] but whoever hates bribes[NOTE:4] will live.
notes: Heb “the one who gains.” The phrase בּוֹצֵעַ בָּצַע (botseaʿ batsaʿ) is a participle followed by its cognate accusative. This refers to a person who is always making the big deal, getting the larger cut, or in a hurry to get rich. The verb, though, makes it clear that the gaining of a profit is by violence and usually unjust, since the root has the idea of “cut off; break off; gain by violence.” The line is contrasted with hating bribes, and so the gain in this line may be through bribery.

The participle “troubles” (עֹכֵר, ʿokher) can have the connotation of making things difficult for the family, or completely ruining the family (cf. NAB). In Josh 7:1 Achan took some of the “banned things” and was put to death: Because he “troubled Israel,” the Lord would “trouble” him (take his life, Josh 7:25).
Heb “his house.”

Heb “gifts” (so KJV). Gifts can be harmless enough, but in a setting like this the idea is that the “gift” is in exchange for some “profit [or, gain].” Therefore they are bribes (cf. ASV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT), and to be hated or rejected. Abram, for example, would not take anything that the king of Sodom had to offer, “lest [he] say, “I have made Abram rich” (Gen 14:22-24).

verses.zh: 义人的心，思量如何回答；恶人的口吐出恶言。
verses.en: The heart[NOTE:1] of the righteous considers[NOTE:2] how[NOTE:3] to answer,[NOTE:4] but the mouth of the wicked pours out evil things.[NOTE:5]
notes: Or “mind.” The term לֵב (lev) can refer to the “mind” or “heart” and represent a person’s thinking, feeling, or will.

The verb יֶהְגֶּה (yehgeh) means “to muse; to meditate; to consider; to study.” It also involves planning, such as with the wicked “planning” a vain thing (Ps 2:1, which is contrasted with the righteous who “meditate” in the law [1:2]).
The word “how” is supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

The LXX reads: “the hearts of the righteous meditate faithfulness.”sn The advice of the proverb is to say less but better things. The wise—here called the righteous—are cautious in how they respond to others. They think about it (heart = mind) before speaking.
The form is plural. What they say (the “mouth” is a metonymy of cause) is any range of harmful things.

verses.zh: 耶和华远离恶人，却听义人的祷告。
verses.en: The Lord is far[NOTE:1] from the wicked,but he hears[NOTE:2] the prayer of the righteous.[NOTE:3]
notes: To say that the Lord is “far” from the wicked is to say that he has made himself unavailable to their appeal—he does not answer them. This motif is used by David throughout Ps 22 for the problem of unanswered prayer—“Why are you far off?”

The verb “hear” (שָׁמַע, shamaʿ) has more of the sense of “respond to” in this context. If one “listens to the voice of the Lord,” for example, it means that he obeys the Lord. If one wishes God to “hear his prayer,” it means he wishes God to answer it.

God’s response to prayer is determined by the righteousness of the one who prays. A prayer of repentance by the wicked is an exception, for by it they would become the righteous (C. H. Toy, Proverbs [ICC], 316).

verses.zh: 眼有光，使心喜乐；好信息，使骨滋润。
verses.en: A bright look[NOTE:1] brings joy to the heart,and good news gives health to the body.[NOTE:2]
notes: The LXX has “the eye that sees beautiful things.” D. W. Thomas suggests pointing מְאוֹר (meʾor) as a Hophal participle, “a fine sight cheers the mind” (“Textual and Philological Notes,” 205). But little is to be gained from this change.tn Heb “light of the eyes” (so KJV, NRSV). The expression may indicate the gleam in the eyes of the one who tells the good news, as the parallel clause suggests.

Heb “makes fat the bones;” NAB “invigorates the bones;” NASB “puts fat on the bones.” The word “bones” is a metonymy of subject, the bones representing the whole body. The idea of “making fat” signifies by comparison (hypocatastasis) with fat things that the body will be healthy and prosperous (e.g., Prov 17:22; 25:25; Gen 45:27-28; Isa 52:7-8). Good news makes the person feel good in body and soul.

verses.zh: 听从生命责备的，必常在智慧人中。
verses.en: The person[NOTE:1] who hears the reproof that leads to life[NOTE:2] is at home[NOTE:3] among the wise.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “ear” (so KJV, NRSV). The term “ear” is a synecdoche of part (= ear) for the whole (= person).
“Life” is an objective genitive: Reproof brings or preserves life. Cf. NIV11 “life-giving correction”; NLT “constructive criticism.”
Heb “lodges.” This means to live with, to be at home with.
The proverb is one full sentence; it affirms that a teachable person is among the wise.

verses.zh: 弃绝管教的，轻看自己的生命；听从责备的，却得智慧。
verses.en: The one who refuses correction despises himself,[NOTE:1] but whoever listens to[NOTE:2] reproof acquires understanding.[NOTE:3]
notes: To “despise oneself” means to reject oneself as if there was little value. The one who ignores discipline is not interested in improving himself.
The nuances of שָׁמַע (shamaʿ) include hearing and obeying or carrying out what was said. Cf. “heeds” so NAB, NIV, NKJV, NRSV.
The term לֵב (lev, “mind, heart”) is used as a metonymy of association for what one does with the mind (thinking), and so refers to discernment, wisdom, good sense.

verses.zh: 敬畏耶和华是智慧的训诲；尊荣以前，必有谦卑。
verses.en: The fear of the Lord provides wise instruction,[NOTE:1] and before honor comes humility.[NOTE:2]
notes: The idea of the first line is similar to Prov 1:7 and 9:10. Here it may mean that the fear of the Lord results from the discipline of wisdom, just as easily as it may mean that the fear of the Lord leads to the discipline of wisdom. The second reading harmonizes with the theme in the book that the fear of the Lord is the starting point.tn Heb “[is] instruction of wisdom” (KJV and NASB similar). The noun translated “wisdom” is an attributive genitive: “wise instruction.”

Heb “[is] humility” (so KJV). The second clause is a parallel idea in that it stresses how one thing leads to another—humility to honor. Humble submission in faith to the Lord brings wisdom and honor.
